about: What every SCE payload reader refuses, and how it names the refusal,
written out by hand (docs/adr/0087, sections 2.3 and 2.4).
A reader that refuses an event's data says why in a sentence each runtime
spells in its own words, and beside the sentence carries the refusal as
data: a code of sce:std/lift/refusal_code.scxml, the place as a strict
RFC 6901 pointer (empty for the whole text, otherwise `/` before each
reference token, `~` written `~0` and `/` written `~1`), and the bound the
value broke for `tooLong` (bytes) and `tooMany` (elements), null for every
other code. The sentences are not compared here; the data is, so that one
text is one refusal on every runtime.
Why a shared table: read in their code on 2026-11-04, the readers disagreed
on what a text is. Python's `json.loads` and Go's `encoding/json` kept the
last value of a repeated name, the C and C++ readers the first, and the
Rust, Kotlin and Swift readers refused it; and the C reader wrote the byte
a `\u0000` escape names into a text it holds NUL-terminated, where the
text ends. A table read by every reader is what holds them to one answer.
Each case gives `data`, the event's data as it arrives; `type`, the type of
its one field `v`, in the form the Interpreter's reader takes
(`"uint8"`, `"string"` for a text with no bound, `["low", "high"]` for
an enum, `{"string": B}`, `{"bytes": B}`, `{"optional": T}`,
`{"list": T, "max": B}`, `{"record": {"id": T}}`); and either
`refusal`, what the reader must refuse the data with, or `accepted: true`
for data the reader must read. A record's fields are read in the order the
table writes them, and no case depends on that order. The bounds are 2, 3
and 8, so a reader whose bounds are fixed when it is compiled reads every
case through one instance per bound.
